content.text: The .NET garbage collector doesn't free objects when you drop a reference. It runs when allocations or memory pressure call for it, finds everything still reachable from its roots and reclaims the rest. Setting a local to
forces a full, blocking collection that usually costs more than it saves. When memory won't come back, find what still references it.
After the nightly import, an ASP.NET Core service's memory graph stays high, so a developer adds

at the end of the import "to free memory sooner." The next night, the graph looks the same. The import also takes longer, and the requests that arrive during it see latency spikes. Two weeks later, a heap snapshot finds the real cause: a static list that keeps every imported batch "for the status page." No amount of nulling or collecting could free memory that was still referenced.
The belief: memory in .NET is freed when you let go of an object, so setting references to
as soon as you're done gets memory back sooner. And if memory still looks high, calling
cleans up and makes the app faster.
It feels like responsible engineering. Developers who came from C++ or COM learned to release every object explicitly, and
looks like the managed version of
. Demos seem to prove it: call
drops. And Task Manager shows a big number that doesn't shrink on its own, which looks like something the code should fix.
The trouble is that the GC doesn't work object by object. It doesn't notice when you drop a reference, and it doesn't wait for permission to run.
The GC looks for what's alive, not for what died
During a collection, the GC starts from its

: static fields, local variables on thread stacks, CPU registers, GC handles and the finalization queue. It follows every reference from there and marks what it reaches. Everything it didn't reach is garbage, and the GC reclaims that space, compacting the survivors when enough garbage is found. So an object isn't freed when you stop using it. It becomes eligible once no path from any root leads to it, and its memory comes back at a later collection.
A collection starts for one of three reasons: allocations pass a threshold the GC keeps adjusting as the process runs, the machine is low on physical memory, or someone calls
triggers nothing. Microsoft's docs are direct about the third reason: in almost all cases you don't need to call it, because the garbage collector runs continuously.

. New objects start in gen 0, which is collected often and quickly, and most objects die there. Survivors are promoted to gen 1, then gen 2. A gen 2 collection is a full collection of the whole heap, and the
, where objects of 85,000 bytes or more live, is collected only with gen 2. The design bets on short lives: a request's temporary objects should die young and cost almost nothing.
For a local variable, the JIT decides how long it counts as a root, and optimizations can shorten or lengthen that window. In optimized code, a local can stop counting right after its last use, so

at the end of a method is usually noise. Nulling matters in exactly one situation: when it removes the last path from a long-lived root. That means a static field, a singleton, a cache entry or an event subscription, not a local that's about to go out of scope anyway. That's also where real leaks live.

performs a full, blocking collection of all generations. Managed threads are suspended while it runs, including the ones serving requests. Every object still alive at that moment, such as the data of in-flight requests, survives and is promoted to an older generation, where it's collected less often and at higher cost. Microsoft's guidance for ASP.NET Core is plain: in general, production apps should not call it.

rows.text: Nothing is freed until a collection runs; nulling helps only if it removes the last path from a root
Nulling locals at the end of a method helps the GC
The JIT already decides when a local stops being a root; the line is noise
It forces a full, blocking collection and promotes everything still alive
High memory in Task Manager means a leak
Server GC lets the heap grow for throughput; a leak is memory that never flattens out
The GC frees objects one by one as they die
It finds what's reachable and reclaims the rest, mostly in cheap gen 0 collections

content.text: ASP.NET Core apps use Server GC by default. It's tuned for throughput, with a heap and a dedicated GC thread per logical CPU, and it can let the heap grow when memory is available. Since .NET 9, a mode called DATAS is on by default for Server GC; it adapts the heap size to the amount of long-lived data and shrinks it when the load drops. So a high but flat working set is often normal. The sign of a leak is memory that keeps rising and never flattens, even after collections.

blocks.title: Find the root, not the object

content.text: When memory won't come back, take a heap snapshot with the Visual Studio memory tools or
and look at the path from a root to the objects that pile up. The answer is almost always a static collection, a cache without limits or an event handler that was never removed.
How to apply it in your project

Give caches a size limit or an expiration, and store summaries instead of full data in anything static or singleton.
Watch the GC heap size and gen 2 collection counts over time with
, and change GC settings only when the numbers point to a real problem.

items.text: The GC reclaims objects that no root can reach, during collections triggered by allocations and memory pressure.
on a local rarely matters; removing the last reference from a static, cache or event is what frees memory.
forces a full, blocking collection and promotes live objects; keep it out of production code.
High memory under Server GC isn't a leak by itself; memory that never flattens is.
To fix a leak, find the root that holds the objects instead of forcing collections.
